Marketing analytics + machine learning

Can we predict the next Spotify hit?

An end-to-end case study using more than 230,000 tracks to examine popularity drivers, identify promising releases, and translate audio profiles into targeted marketing strategies.

01 · Business context

Millions of tracks compete for limited attention.

Streaming platforms, record labels, and marketing teams must choose which songs receive playlist placement, recommendation exposure, and promotional investment. Audio characteristics offer useful signals, but commercial success is also shaped by artist visibility, timing, social momentum, and marketing execution.

The decision problem

Promotional resources are limited. Investing in the wrong releases wastes budget, while overlooking a promising track can mean missing a major opportunity.

Which tracks deserve a closer look before the campaign begins?

My analytical response

I used three complementary methods rather than forcing one model to answer every question.

Regression quantified popularity drivers. Classification screened potential hits. Clustering created marketable track segments.

My role: Data preparation, exploratory analysis, machine learning implementation, evaluation, business interpretation, and portfolio case-study development.
02 · Project goals

Three business questions. Three analytical tools.

GOAL 01

Predict popularity

Estimate the 0–100 popularity score and identify the direction of each audio feature's relationship with success.

GOAL 02

Identify potential hits

Classify releases as hit or non-hit to support an early go or no-go promotional review.

GOAL 03

Segment the catalog

Discover natural audio profiles and translate them into targeting and positioning strategies.

Exploratory analysis: Popularity was unevenly distributed, energy and loudness were strongly related, and acousticness generally moved in the opposite direction.

Data quality decisions

The original dataset contained 232,725 rows. I removed one incomplete track name and more than 55,000 duplicate track IDs, leaving 176,773 unique observations.

Model preparation

Categorical features were encoded, numerical inputs were standardized where needed, and a binary hit variable was engineered using a popularity threshold of 50.

04 · Machine learning

Each model answers a different decision.

Model 01

Multiple linear regression

Business question: How popular might a track become, and which audio features influence the estimate?

The model explained roughly 20% of popularity variance. This is meaningful enough for early screening, but it also demonstrates that audio alone cannot capture artist reach, playlist placement, marketing spend, or cultural momentum.

0.20 R²
15.57 RMSE
~12.5 MAE
Model 02

Logistic regression

Business question: Is this release promising enough to enter a more detailed promotional review?

A threshold of 70 initially produced misleading 97.8% accuracy because only 2.2% of tracks qualified as hits. Lowering the threshold to 50 and balancing class weights created a more useful model focused on catching real opportunities.

75.2% recall
62.0% accuracy
0.478 F1
Why recall matters: For release screening, reviewing extra candidates is less costly than failing to surface a track with real commercial potential.
Model 03

K-Means clustering

Business question: Which audience and campaign context best fits each track?

Eight audio dimensions were standardized and grouped into five distinct profiles. The clusters were then interpreted through segmentation, targeting, and go-to-market positioning.

5 segments
40.7 top average popularity
Feel-Good Dance

High danceability and valence. Position for social, party, and upbeat lifestyle playlists.

High-Energy Electronic

Strong energy and intensity. Target workouts, nightlife, gaming, and festival contexts.

Soft Acoustic Pop

Higher acousticness and a gentler profile. Match to coffee, focus, and relaxed discovery playlists.

Ambient Instrumental

Instrumental and atmospheric. Position for concentration, wellness, and background listening.

Spoken Word / Live

Higher speech or live-presence signals. Use context-driven placement rather than mass promotion.

05 · Model comparison

Useful signals, not a crystal ball.

Linear regression

0.20 R²

Best for understanding directional relationships and benchmarking likely popularity.

Logistic regression

75% recall

Best for high-recall release screening when missing a possible hit is costly.

K-Means

5 segments

Best for tailoring audience, playlist, message, and campaign context.

Across the three models, danceability, loudness, and energy repeatedly emerged as useful commercial signals, while the modest predictive power reinforced the need for external market data.
06 · Business recommendations

Turn model output into marketing decisions.

Use hit prediction as a screening tool

Automatically flag high-potential tracks for human review rather than treating the classifier as an autonomous release decision.

Prioritize high-value segments

Direct more campaign testing toward feel-good dance and high-energy electronic profiles while avoiding blanket promotion across the entire catalog.

Match campaigns to listening context

Align tracks with the moment in which listeners are most likely to engage: workouts, social settings, focus, relaxation, or discovery.

Expand beyond audio features

Add artist followers, playlist history, release timing, social activity, marketing spend, and prior performance to improve decision quality.

07 · Technical implementation

Built with an interpretable Python workflow.

The project emphasized transparent preprocessing, explainable models, and business-facing evaluation rather than chasing a single headline accuracy number.

What I would improve next

Test tree-based and gradient boosting models, use cross-validation and hyperparameter tuning, add SHAP explanations, and validate performance on newer data.

Most important lesson

A technically correct model is not automatically useful. Threshold selection, class imbalance, business costs, and the decision context determine whether a metric has real value.

Conclusion

Audio data cannot guarantee the next global hit, but it can reduce uncertainty.

Used responsibly, these models can help marketing teams screen releases, identify stronger promotional candidates, position tracks by listening context, and focus limited resources where they are most likely to create value. The strongest future system would combine audio features with artist, playlist, social, and campaign data.
